questions.q: A frictionless circular wire of unit radius is fixed on the horizontal plane. Two point particles of unit mass start moving simultaneously from point $A\left(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ with identical uniform angular speeds in opposite directions, and meet again at point $B\left(\theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. During this time, which of the following figures schematically represent the magnitude of the total linear momentum $P$ of the system, as a function of $\theta$ ?
questions.solution:
Let the uniform angular speed of the particles be $\omega$.

The position vector of the particle on the right at an angle $\theta$ is given by $\vec{r}_1 = \cos\theta \hat{i} + \sin\theta \hat{j}$.

Since it moves from $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, its angular velocity is $\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = -\omega$.

The velocity of the first particle is $\vec{v}_1 = \dfrac{d\vec{r}_1}{dt} = (-\sin\theta \hat{i} + \cos\theta \hat{j})\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \omega\sin\theta \hat{i} - \omega\cos\theta \hat{j}$.

By symmetry, the position vector of the particle on the left is $\vec{r}_2 = -\cos\theta \hat{i} + \sin\theta \hat{j}$.

Its velocity is $\vec{v}_2 = \dfrac{d\vec{r}_2}{dt} = (\sin\theta \hat{i} + \cos\theta \hat{j})\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = -\omega\sin\theta \hat{i} - \omega\cos\theta \hat{j}$.

The total linear momentum of the system is $\vec{P} = m\vec{v}_1 + m\vec{v}_2$.

Given $m = 1$, we have $\vec{P} = (\omega\sin\theta \hat{i} - \omega\cos\theta \hat{j}) + (-\omega\sin\theta \hat{i} - \omega\cos\theta \hat{j}) = -2\omega\cos\theta \hat{j}$.

The magnitude of the total linear momentum is $P = |\vec{P}| = 2\omega\cos\theta$ (since $\cos\theta \geq 0$ for $\theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$).

The graph of $P$ versus $\theta$ is a cosine curve which is zero at $\theta = \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and maximum at $\theta = 0$. This corresponds to the fourth graph.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R),
Assertion (A):
When a fire cracker (rocket) explodes in mid air, its fragments fly in such a way that they continue moving in the same path, which the fire cracker would have followed, had it not exploded
Reason (R):
Explosion of cracker (rocket) occurs due to internal forces only and no external force acts for this explosion.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of $(A)$
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of $(\mathrm{A})$
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
As per Newton's II law for a system
\(\vec{F}_{\text {external }}=\frac{d \vec{P}}{d t}=m \frac{d \vec{v} \text { oam }}{d t}\)
As explosion occurs due to internal forces only, the velocity of centre of mass would remain unchanged. This means that the centre of mass would continue to travel along same path as it was moving before explosion.
The fragments can however move individually along various directions.
Thus (A) is not correct and (R) is correct.

questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(i) Centre of mass of a body always coincides with the centre of gravity of the body.

(ii) Centre of mass of a body is the point at which the total gravitational torque on the body is zero

(iii) A couple on a body produce both translational and rotational motion in a body.

(iv) Mechanical advantage greater than one means that small effort can be used to lift a large load.
questions.solution:
(i) Centre of gravity coincides with centre of mass for bodies when gravitational field is uniform (usually for bodies of small height).

(ii) Since the gravitational force can be assumed to be centred at the centre of gravity, so torque of gravitational force about the centre of gravity must be zero. In mechanics, usually we deal with the objects of small height for which torque of gravitational force about centre of mass will also be zero.

(iii) Couple produces only rotational motion.

(iv) Mechanical advantage =LoadEffort>1 ⇒Load>Effort

questions.q: Bob $B$ of mass $m$ at rest is hanging vertically from the ceiling via a massless string of length $10$ m, as shown in the figure. Point mass $A$ of mass $m$ travelling horizontally with speed $10$ ms$^{-1}$ hits bob $B$ elastically. The bob $B$ rises $h$ meter after the collision. Taking the acceleration due to gravity $g=10$ ms$^{-2}$ and neglecting the size of the bob, the value of $h$ is :
questions.solution:
Since the collision is elastic and the masses of $A$ and $B$ are equal, they will exchange their velocities upon collision.

Velocity of bob $B$ just after the collision, $v = 10$ ms$^{-1}$.

By conservation of mechanical energy for bob $B$ during its upward swing:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = m g h$

Substituting the given values ($v = 10$ ms$^{-1}$, $g = 10$ ms$^{-2}$):

$\dfrac{1}{2} \times m \times (10)^2 = m \times 10 \times h$

$50 = 10 h$

$h = 5$ m.

Since $h \lt L$ (where $L = 10$ m), the string does not become slack and the bob reaches a maximum height of $5$ m.

Answer: $5$

questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : Quick collisions are more violent than slow collisions.
Reason (R) : Quick collision are inelastic in nature.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion is correct because in quick collision time duration will be less due to which higher impulse will act on a body.
Reason is false because collision may be both elastic or inelastic.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Assertion : Centre of mass of a system may or may not lie inside the system.
Reason : The position of centre of mass depends on distribution of mass within the system.
options: If both Assertion & Reason are true and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
If both Assertion & Reason are true but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
If Assertion is true statement but Reason is false.
If both Assertion and Reason are false statements.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): True. The centre of mass (COM) can lie inside or outside the material of the body/system. Examples: for a uniform ring or a semicircular wire, the COM lies at the geometric center-which is empty space.
- Reason (R): True. The COM position is determined by the mass distribution:
\(\vec{R}_{C M}=\frac{\sum m_i \vec{r} i}{\sum m_i} \quad \text { or } \quad \vec{R} C M=\frac{1}{M} \int \vec{r} d m\)
Change how mass is spread, and the COM shifts accordingly.
- Does R explain A? Yes. Because COM depends on how mass is distributed, certain distributions (like mass arranged around a hole) naturally place the COM in a region with no material, explaining why COM may be outside the system.
Hence, both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A \(\rightarrow\) Option (1).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Assertion : The position of centre of mass relative to body is independent of the choice of coordinate system.
Reason : Centre of mass does not shift its position in the absence of an external force.
options: If both Assertion & Reason are true and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
If both Assertion & Reason are true but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
If Assertion is true statement but Reason is false.
If both Assertion and Reason are false statements.
questions.solution:
Changing the coordinate system adds the same offset to all position vectors. The COM position relative to the body (i.e., measured from the body's own geometry) doesn't depend on the coordinate choice.
- Reason (R): False (as stated).
With no external force, the COM has zero acceleration, not zero motion. It can still move at constant velocity; so its position can change with time unless it happened to be at rest initially in that frame.
Therefore, A is true, R is false \(\rightarrow\) Option (3).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Two particles mass \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are kept at rest at \(t=0\). They start attracting each other due to their gravitational pull, then
Statement-I: The total momentum of the system is zero at any instant.
Statement-II: Both the particles gain equal momentum in opposite direction in equal interval of time as both are acted upon equal and opposite forces.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
1. By Newton's third law the internal forces are equal and opposite:
\(\mathrm{F}_{12}=-\mathrm{F}_{21} .\)
If \(\mathrm{p}_1, \mathrm{p}_2\) are momenta, then
\(\frac{d \mathrm{p}_1}{d t}=\mathrm{F}_{12}, \quad \frac{d \mathrm{p}_2}{d t}=\mathrm{F}_{21}=-\mathrm{F}_{12} .\)
Add them:
\(\frac{d}{d t}\left(\mathrm{p}_1+\mathrm{p}_2\right)=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{p}_1+\mathrm{p}_2=\text { constant }\)
Initially both particles are at rest, so \(\mathrm{p}_1+\mathrm{p}_2=\mathrm{0}\). Hence at every later time the total momentum remains zero. This proves Statement I.
2. From the pair of equations above,
\(\frac{d \mathrm{p}_1}{d t}=-\frac{d \mathrm{p}_2}{d t} .\)
Integrating over any equal time interval gives
\(\Delta \mathrm{p}_1=-\Delta \mathrm{p}_2,\)
i.e. they gain equal magnitude momenta in opposite directions (even though their velocities will be different if \(m_1 \neq m_2\)). That proves Statement II.
Both statements are therefore true (and Statement II \(\downarrow\) ist the differential form of the same Newton-third law fact that ensures Statement J).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Statement-I: A point particle of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) collides with stationary point particle of mass \(M\). If the maximum energy loss possible is given as \(f\left(\frac{1}{2} m v^2\right)\) then \(f=\left(\frac{m}{M+m}\right)\).
Statement-II: Maximum energy loss occurs when the particles get stuck together as a result of the collision.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
Initial kinetic energy
\(K_i=\frac{1}{2} m v^2\)
If after collision the two masses stick (perfectly inelastic), common velocity by momentum conservation is
\(V=\frac{m v}{m+M}\)
Final kinetic energy then is
\(K_f=\frac{1}{2}(m+M) V^2=\frac{1}{2}(m+M) \frac{m^2 v^2}{(m+M)^2}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{m^2 v^2}{m+M}\)
Energy lost:
\(\Delta K=K_i-K_f=\frac{1}{2} m v^2-\frac{1}{2} \frac{m^2 v^2}{m+M}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2\left(1-\frac{m}{m+M}\right)=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \cdot \frac{M}{m+M}\)
So the maximum fractional loss \(f\) (such that \(\Delta K=f \cdot \frac{1}{2} m v^2\)) is
\(f=\frac{M}{m+M}\)
Thus Statement-I (which asserts \(f=\frac{m}{m+M}\)) is wrong. Statement-II is correct because the maximum kinetic energy loss occurs for the perfectly inelastic case (particles stick, \(e=0\)).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Statement-I: Two particles moving in the same direction do not lose all their energy in a completely inelastic collision.
Statement-II: Principle of conservation of momentum holds true for all kinds of collisions.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
Let masses \(m_1, m_2\) have initial velocities \(u_1, u_2\) in the same direction and they stick after collision (perfectly, inelastic). Common velocity
\(v=\frac{m_1 u_1+m_2 u_2}{m_1+m_2}\)
Initial KE:
\(K_i=\frac{1}{2} m_1 u_1^2+\frac{1}{2} m_2 u_2^2,\)
Final KE:
\(K_f=\frac{1}{2}\left(m_1+m_2\right) v^2\)
Loss of kinetic energy
\(\Delta K=K_i-K_f=\frac{1}{2} \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1+m_2}\left(u_1-u_2\right)^2 \geq 0\)
This loss is not the whole initial energy except when \(u_1=u_2\) (then \(\Delta K=0\)). So Statement-1 is true: they do not lose all their energy in general.
Statement-II is also true: momentum is conserved in all collisions provided the system is isolated (no externa impulse). That includes elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic collisions and explosions (internal forces only).
So both are true \(\rightarrow\) option (1).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Statement-I: When you lean behind over the hind legs of the chair, the chair falls back after a certain angle.
Statement-II: Centre of mass lying outside the system makes the system unstable.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
- Stability criterion: an object is stable as long as the vertical line through its centre of mass (CM) falls inside the base of support. If the vertical from the CM passes outside the base, the normal reaction can no longer provide a balancing moment and the object will tip.
- Apply to the chair. when you lean back on the hind legs you tilt the chair so the projection of the combined CM (you + chair) moves toward the back edge of the base. At a certain tilt angle the vertical through the CM crosses the rear edge - beyond that the CM lies outside the support polygon and the chair rotates (falls) backward. That is exactly Statement-I and it follows from Statement-II.
So both statements are true and related: the chair falls when the CM's vertical leaves the base of support.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Assertion (A): During collision between two objects, the momentum of colliding objects is conserved only in direction perpendicular to line of impact.
Reason (R): The force on colliding objects in perpendicular direction to line of impact is zero.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A):
"During collision between two objects, the momentum of colliding objects is conserved only in direction perpendicular to line of impact."
This is false.
- In reality, linear momentum is conserved in all directions (because external force is absent).
- What is special is that along the line of impact, momentum is not separately conserved for each object (because of impulsive forces), but the total system momentum is always conserved in both perpendicular and parallel directions.
Reason (R):
"The force on colliding objects in perpendicular direction to line of impact is zero."
This is true.
- Collision forces act only along the line of impact (normal at contact).
- Therefore, perpendicular to line of impact, no impulsive force acts.
\(\checkmark\) So the correct choice is:
(4) Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
That matches the given answer key.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Assertion (A): In an elastic collision of two bodies, the momentum and energy of each body is conserved.
Reason (R): If two bodies stick to each other, after colliding, the collision is said to be perfectly inelastic.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A) is False.
- In an elastic collision, the total momentum of the system and the total kinetic energy of the system are conserved. Momentum and kinetic energy are not, in general, conserved for each body individually; they can exchange between bodies. So the phrase "of each body" makes A false.
- Reason (R) is True.
- When two bodies stick together after collision, the collision is perfectly inelastic by definition.
Therefore, the correct option is (4): Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Assertion (A): In inelastic collision, a part of kinetic energy convert into heat energy, sound energy and light energy etc.
Reason (R): The force of interaction in an inelastic collision is non-conservative in nature.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A) is True. In an inelastic collision, total momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy of the system decreases because some of it is transformed into other forms (heat, sound, internal energy due to deformation).
- Reason (R) is True. The contact/deformation forces during an inelastic collision include non-conservative components (e.g., frictional and internal dissipative forces), so mechanical energy is not conserved.
- However, R is not the correct explanation for A in the strict assertion-reason sense: A states what happens to kinetic energy; R states a property of the forces but does not explicitly link how this causes the conversion into heat/sound/etc. Hence it's true but not a direct explanatory statement for A .
Correct option: (2) Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Assertion (A): In an elastic collision between two bodies, the energy of each body is conserved.
Reason (R): The total energy of an isolated system is conserved.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A) is False. In an elastic collision, what is conserved is the total kinetic energy of the system and total momentum. The kinetic energy and momentum of each individual body generally change due to exchange during collision; they are not conserved body-by-body.
- Reason (R) is True. For an isolated system, total energy (including kinetic, potential, internal, etc.) is conserved.
Therefore, the correct option is (4): Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Choose correct statement
(A) The position of centre of mass of a system is dependent on the choice of coordinate system.
(B) Newton's second law of motion is applicable to the centre of mass of the system.
(C) Internal forces can not change the state of centre of mass.
(D) Internal forces can change the state of centre of mass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
A body \(A\) moving with momentum \(P\) collides one-dimensionally with another stationary body \(B\) of same mass. During impact, \(A\) gives impulse \(J\) to \(B\). Then which of the following is/are correct?
(a) The total momentum of \(A\) and \(B\) is \(P\) before and after impact and \((P-J)\) during the impact.
(b) During the impact, \(B\) gives impulse of magnitude \(J\) to \(A\).
(c) The coefficient of restitution is \(\left[\frac{2 J}{P}-1\right]\).
(d) The coefficient of restitution is \(\left[\frac{2 J}{P}+1\right]\).
questions.solution:
According to the question, a collision between two bodies (\(A\) and \(B\)) is shown in the figure below,
So, the coefficient of restitution \(\begin{aligned} e & =\frac{\text { Relative velocity of separation }}{\text { Relative velocity of approach }} \\ \Rightarrow \quad e & =\frac{\frac{J-p}{m}+\frac{J}{m}}{\frac{p}{m}-0}=\frac{2 J}{P}-1 \quad\left(\because v=\frac{m v}{m}=\frac{p}{m}\right) \end{aligned}\) During the impact, \(B\) gives impulse \(J_B=p+J-p=J\) Hence, the statement (b) and (c) are correct.

A projectile is projected at a speed u at an angle \(\theta\) with horizontal. At the highest point projectile splits into two fragments of mass ratio \(1: 2\). The smaller fragment coming to rest. Then consider following statements :-

Which of the following is correct?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
A particle of mass m moving with a velocity \((3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\) collides with stationary body of mass M and finally moves with velocity \((-2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\) then
(A) Impulse received by \(m=m(5 \hat{i}-5 \hat{j})\)
(B) Impulse received by \(m=m(-5 \hat{i}-\hat{j})\)
(C) Impulse received by \(\mathrm{M}=\mathrm{m}(5 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}})\)
(D) Impulse received by \(M=m(5 \hat{i}-\hat{j})\) then correct statements are
questions.solution:
\(\begin{aligned}
& I=m \cdot \Delta v \\
& =m[(-2 \hat{i}+\hat{j})-(3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j})] \\
& =m[-5 \hat{i}-\hat{j}] \rightarrow \text { Impulse on } m \\
& \text { Impulse on } M=-(\text {Impulse on } m) \\
& =m(5 \hat{i}+\hat{j})
\end{aligned}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Match the following columns with respective positions of centre of mass -
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline & \text{Column - I} & & \text{Column - II} \\
\hline \text{(A)} & \text{uniform rod length } =\mathrm{R} & \text{(P)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{3 \mathrm{R}}{8} \\
\hline \text{(B)} & \begin{array}{l} \text{uniform thin semicircular} \\ \text{ring of radius } R \end{array} & \text{(Q)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2} \\
\hline \text{(C)} & \begin{array}{l} \text{unifiorm semicurcula} \\ \text{disc of radius } R \end{array} & \text{(R)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{4 \mathrm{R}}{3 \pi} \\
\hline \text{(D)} & \begin{array}{l} \text{uniform solid hemisphere} \\ \text{of radius } R \end{array} & \text{(S)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{2 \mathrm{R}}{\pi} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
options: \(A: P, B: R, C: Q, D: S\)
\(A: Q, B: P, C: R, D: S\)
\(A: Q, B: S, C: R, D: P\)
questions.solution:
(A) Uniform rod of length \(R\)
- For a uniform rod, the COM lies exactly at the midpoint.
So, \(x=\frac{R}{2}\).
That matches (Q).
(B) Uniform thin semicircular ring of radius R
- Standard result: COM of a semicircular ring lies at a distance \(\frac{2 R}{\pi}\) from the center, along symmetry axis.
So, \(x=\frac{2 R}{\pi}\).
That matches (S).
(C) Uniform semicircular disc of radius R
- Standard result: COM of a semicircular lamina is at a distance \(\frac{4 R}{3 \pi}\) from the center along symmetry axis.
So, \(x=\frac{4 R}{3 \pi}\).
That matches (R).
(D) Uniform solid hemisphere of radius R
- Standard result: COM of a solid hemisphere is at a distance \(\frac{3 R}{8}\) from the flat face (base).
So, \(x=\frac{3 R}{8}\).
That matches (P).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Particle of mass m, kinetic energy K and momentum P collides head on elastically with another particle of mass 2 m at rest. After collision:
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|c|}
\hline & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline \text{(A)} & \text{Momentum of } \mathrm{I}^{\text {st }} \text{ particle} & \text{(P)} & \frac{4}{3} \mathrm{P} \\
\hline \text{(B)} & \text{Momentum of } \mathrm{II}^{\text {rd }} \text{ particle} & \text{(Q)} & \frac{\mathrm{K}}{9} \\
\hline \text{(C)} & \mathrm{KE}^{\text {of }} \mathrm{I}^{\text {sd }} \text{ particle} & \text{(R)} & \frac{8 \mathrm{~K}}{9} \\
\hline \text{(D)} & \mathrm{KE}^{\text {of }} \mathrm{II}^{\text {rd }} \text{ particle} & \text{(S)} & -\frac{\mathrm{P}}{3} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution: \(v_1 ~\&~ v_2\) are velocities after collision Conservation of linear momentum \(\begin{gathered} \mathrm{mu}=\mathrm{mv}_1+2 \mathrm{mv}_2 \\ \mathrm{u}=\mathrm{v}_1+\mathrm{v}_2 \quad \ldots (1) \\ \mathrm{e}=1=\frac{\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{u}} \\ \mathrm{u}=\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1 \quad \ldots (2) \end{gathered}\) From (1) & (2) \(v_2=\frac{2 u}{3} ; v_1=-\frac{u}{3}\) Momentum of \(1^{\text {t }}\) particle \(=-\frac{\mathrm{mu}}{3}=-\frac{\mathrm{P}}{3}\) Momentum of \(2^{\text {nd }}\) particle \(=+2 \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{u}}{3}\right)=\frac{4 \mathrm{P}}{3}\) K.E. of \(1^a\) particle \(=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}}{3}\right)^2=\frac{\mathrm{K}}{9}\) K.E. of \(2^{\infty}\) particle \(=\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{u}}{3}\right)^2=\frac{8 \mathrm{~K}}{9}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Four point masses are placed at four corners of a square of side 4 m as shown in the figure. Match the following columns.
\(\begin{array}{l|l|l|l} & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\ \hline \text { (A) } & \begin{array}{l} x \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 4 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 2 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (p) } & (7 / 2) \mathrm{m} \\ \text { (B) } & \begin{array}{l} x \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 4 \mathrm{~kg}, 2 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 3 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (q) } & 4 / 3 \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { (C) } & \begin{array}{l} y \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 1 \mathrm{~kg}, 4 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 3 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (r) } & 3 \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { (D) } & \begin{array}{l} y \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 1 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 3 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (s) } & \text { (20/9) } \mathrm{m} \\ \hline \end{array}\)
questions.solution:
Formulas:
- x-coordinate of COM: \(x=\Sigma(m i x i) / \Sigma(m i)\)
- \(y\)-coordinate of COM: \(\bar{y}=\Sigma(m \mathrm{i} \mathrm{yi}) / \Sigma(m \mathrm{i})\)
Corner coordinates used above.
A. x-coordinate of COM of 4 kg and 2 kg :
- Masses at \((0,4)\) and \((4,0) \rightarrow x^{-}=(4 \cdot 0+2 \cdot 4) /(4+2)=8 / 6=4 / 3 \mathrm{~m}\).
B. x-coordinate of COM of \(4 \mathrm{~kg}, 2 \mathrm{~kg}\), and 3 kg :
- Positions: \((0,4),(4,0),(4,4)\)
- \(x^{-}=(4 \cdot 0+2 \cdot 4+3 \cdot 4) /(4+2+3)=(0+8+12) / 9=20 / 9 \mathrm{~m}\).
C. y -coordinate of COM of \(1 \mathrm{~kg}, 4 \mathrm{~kg}\), and 3 kg :
- Positions: \((0,0),(0,4),(4,4)\)
- \(y=(1.0+4.4+3.4) /(1+4+3)=(0+16+12) / 8=28 / 8=7 / 2 \mathrm{~m}\).
D. y -coordinate of COM of 1 kg and 3 kg :
- Positions: \((0,0),(4,4)\)
- \(\bar{y}=(1.0+3.4) /(1+3)=12 / 4=3 \mathrm{~m}\).
Thus, matching to options set:
- (p) \(7 / 2 \mathrm{~m}\), (q) \(4 / 3 \mathrm{~m}\), (r) 3 m, (s) 20/9 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Match the following:
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline \text { A. } & \text { Elastic collision } & \text { P. } & e=0 \\
\hline \text { B. } & \text { Inelastic collision } & \text { Q. } & O \lt  e \lt  1 \\
\hline \text { C. } & \text { Explosion } & \text { R. } & e=1 \\
\hline \text { D. } & \text { Plastic collision } & \text { S. } & \text { Final K.E. }\gt \text { initial K.E } \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
(A) Elastic collision
- By definition, perfectly elastic collision has coefficient of restitution \(e=1\).
\((A) \rightarrow(R)\).
(B) Inelastic collision
- For inelastic collisions (not perfectly plastic), coefficient of restitution lies between \(0 \lt  e \lt  1\).
\(\sim(B) \rightarrow(Q)\).
(C) Explosion
- In an explosion, internal energy is released, so Final K.E. > Initial K.E.
\(\sim(C) \rightarrow(S)\).
(D) Plastic collision (perfectly inelastic)
- In a perfectly plastic collision, bodies stick together, so \(e=0\).
\(\sim(\mathrm{D}) \rightarrow(\mathrm{P})\).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A moving particle of mass $m$ collides head-on and elastically with a stationary particle of mass $M$ (where $M \gt  m$). If the moving particle transfers $64\%$ of its initial kinetic energy to the stationary particle, the ratio $\dfrac{M}{m}$ is
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity of the moving particle be $u$.

For a perfectly elastic head-on collision with a stationary target, the fraction of kinetic energy transferred from the projectile to the target is given by:
$f = \dfrac{4mM}{(m + M)^2}$

Given that $64\%$ of the initial kinetic energy is transferred:
$\dfrac{4mM}{(m + M)^2} = \dfrac{64}{100} = \dfrac{16}{25}$

Dividing numerator and denominator by $m^2$ and letting the ratio $\dfrac{M}{m} = x$:
$\dfrac{4x}{(1 + x)^2} = \dfrac{16}{25}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{x}{1 + 2x + x^2} = \dfrac{4}{25}$

Cross-multiplying gives:
$25x = 4 + 8x + 4x^2$

$4x^2 - 17x + 4 = 0$

Solving this quadratic equation:
$4x^2 - 16x - x + 4 = 0$
$4x(x - 4) - 1(x - 4) = 0$
$(4x - 1)(x - 4) = 0$

Thus, $x = 4$ or $x = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Since it is given that $M \gt m$, the ratio $\dfrac{M}{m}$ must be greater than $1$. Therefore, the correct ratio is $4$.

Answer: $4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A point mass of $1$ kg moving horizontally with speed $u$ hits a pendulum bob of mass $2$ kg initially at rest. The collision is perfectly elastic. After the collision, the pendulum bob swings upwards and reaches a maximum vertical height of $0.8$ m. Taking $g = 10$ ms$^{-2}$, the initial speed $u$ of the $1$ kg mass is:
questions.solution:
First, find the velocity of the $2$ kg bob just after the collision using conservation of mechanical energy during its upward swing:

$\dfrac{1}{2} M v_M^2 = M g h$

$v_M = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 0.8} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ ms$^{-1}$.

For a 1D elastic collision, the velocity of a target mass $M$ initially at rest, struck by a mass $m$ moving with initial velocity $u$, is given by:

$v_M = \dfrac{2m}{m + M} u$

Substituting the given values ($m = 1$ kg, $M = 2$ kg, $v_M = 4$ ms$^{-1}$):

$4 = \dfrac{2 \times 1}{1 + 2} u$

$4 = \dfrac{2}{3} u$

$u = 6$ ms$^{-1}$.

Answer: $6$ ms$^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
A ball of mass $m$ moving with speed $v$ strikes a rigid surface. Match the collision scenarios in List-I with the magnitude of impulse imparted to the ball in List-II.

(A)Strikes normally and rebounds perfectly(I)$mv$
(B)Strikes at $30^\circ$ to the normal and rebounds perfectly(II)$2mv$
(C)Strikes at $60^\circ$ to the normal and rebounds perfectly(III)$\sqrt{3}mv$
(D)Strikes at $45^\circ$ to the normal and rebounds perfectly(IV)$\sqrt{2}mv$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
When a ball strikes a rigid surface at an angle $\theta$ with the normal and rebounds perfectly (elastically) with the same speed $v$ at the same angle, the change in momentum is only along the normal direction.

The magnitude of impulse imparted is given by:
$J = |\Delta p| = 2mv \cos\theta$

(A) Strikes normally ($\theta = 0^\circ$):
$J = 2mv \cos(0^\circ) = 2mv$ (Matches II)

(B) Strikes at $30^\circ$ to the normal ($\theta = 30^\circ$):
$J = 2mv \cos(30^\circ) = 2mv \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \sqrt{3}mv$ (Matches III)

(C) Strikes at $60^\circ$ to the normal ($\theta = 60^\circ$):
$J = 2mv \cos(60^\circ) = 2mv \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = mv$ (Matches I)

(D) Strikes at $45^\circ$ to the normal ($\theta = 45^\circ$):
$J = 2mv \cos(45^\circ) = 2mv \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \sqrt{2}mv$ (Matches IV)

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A boy of mass $m$ running horizontally with a velocity $v$ jumps onto a stationary skateboard of mass $2m$. If they move together after the jump, what is the final velocity of the boy and skateboard system?
questions.solution:
Using the principle of conservation of linear momentum:

Initial momentum of the system = Final momentum of the system

The initial momentum is only due to the boy, as the skateboard is stationary:
$p_i = m v + (2m)(0) = m v$

After the jump, the boy and the skateboard move together with a common velocity $v_f$. The total mass is $m + 2m = 3m$.
Final momentum:
$p_f = (3m) v_f$

Equating initial and final momentum:
$m v = 3m v_f$

$v_f = \dfrac{v}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{v}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A moving object of mass $3\text{ kg}$ and velocity $(4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ breaks into two pieces of masses $1\text{ kg}$ and $2\text{ kg}$. If the $1\text{ kg}$ piece moves with a velocity of $(4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ immediately after the explosion, the kinetic energy released during the explosion is
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of linear momentum:
$\vec{P}_{initial} = \vec{P}_{final}$
$M\vec{v} = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2$

Substituting the given values:
$3(4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}) = 1(4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) + 2\vec{v}_2$
$12\hat{i} + 12\hat{j} = 4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\vec{v}_2$
$2\vec{v}_2 = (12 - 4)\hat{i} + (12 + 2)\hat{j}$
$2\vec{v}_2 = 8\hat{i} + 14\hat{j}$
$\vec{v}_2 = 4\hat{i} + 7\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$

Now, calculate the initial kinetic energy ($K_i$):
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} M |\vec{v}|^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (4^2 + 4^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 32 = 48\text{ J}$

Calculate the final kinetic energy ($K_f$):
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2} m_1 |\vec{v}_1|^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} m_2 |\vec{v}_2|^2$
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times (4^2 + (-2)^2) + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (4^2 + 7^2)$
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}(16 + 4) + 1(16 + 49)$
$K_f = 10 + 65 = 75\text{ J}$

The kinetic energy released in the explosion is the increase in kinetic energy:
$\Delta K = K_f - K_i = 75\text{ J} - 48\text{ J} = 27\text{ J}$.

Answer: $27\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A fixed smooth wedge has two faces, each inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. Two identical blocks, each of mass $m$, are released simultaneously from rest at the top vertex and slide down the opposite faces. What should be the value of $\theta$ so that the magnitude of the total linear momentum of the two-block system at any time $t$ is exactly equal to the momentum a single block of mass $m$ would acquire if dropped freely for the same time $t$?
questions.solution:
Let the speed of each block at time $t$ be $v$. Since they slide down smooth inclines of angle $\theta$, their acceleration is $a = g\sin\theta$.

The speed at time $t$ is $v = (g\sin\theta)t$.

The velocity vectors of the two blocks are directed downwards along the inclines. Their horizontal components are equal and opposite, thus cancelling each other out. Their vertical components are both directed downwards with magnitude $v\sin\theta$.

The magnitude of the total linear momentum of the system is $P = 2m(v\sin\theta) = 2m(g\sin\theta t)\sin\theta = 2mgt\sin^2\theta$.

The momentum of a single block of mass $m$ falling freely for time $t$ is $p = mgt$.

Equating the two momenta: $2mgt\sin^2\theta = mgt$

$\sin^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\theta = 45^\circ$.

If one incorrectly assumes the total momentum is simply $2mv$ without resolving into components, they would get $2mgt\sin\theta = mgt \Rightarrow \theta = 30^\circ$.

Answer: $45^\circ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: An object moving in a two-dimensional plane with an initial velocity $(-\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ explodes into two fragments. Immediately after the explosion, the velocity of the first fragment is $(5\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ and the velocity of the second fragment is $(-5\hat{i} + 8\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$. The ratio of the mass of the first fragment to the mass of the second fragment is
questions.solution:
Let the masses of the two fragments be $m_1$ and $m_2$.

According to the law of conservation of linear momentum, the total momentum before the explosion is equal to the total momentum after the explosion:
$(m_1 + m_2)\vec{v} = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2$

Substituting the given velocity vectors:
$(m_1 + m_2)(-\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}) = m_1(5\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) + m_2(-5\hat{i} + 8\hat{j})$

Equating the $\hat{i}$ components on both sides:
$-(m_1 + m_2) = 5m_1 - 5m_2$
$-m_1 - m_2 = 5m_1 - 5m_2$
$4m_2 = 6m_1$
$\dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Equating the $\hat{j}$ components yields the same result:
$4(m_1 + m_2) = -2m_1 + 8m_2$
$4m_1 + 4m_2 = -2m_1 + 8m_2$
$6m_1 = 4m_2$
$\dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Thus, the ratio of their masses is $2:3$.

Answer: $2:3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A body is moving uniformly in a straight line. If its kinetic energy is $24 \mathrm{~J}$ and its linear momentum is $12 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, the distance covered by the body in $5 \mathrm{~s}$ is:
questions.solution:
Given,
Kinetic energy, $K = 24 \mathrm{~J}$
Linear momentum, $p = 12 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
Time, $t = 5 \mathrm{~s}$

The relationship between kinetic energy and linear momentum is:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2} p v$

Rearranging for velocity $v$:
$v = \dfrac{2K}{p}$
$v = \dfrac{2 \times 24}{12} = 4 \mathrm{~m/s}$

The distance covered in $5 \mathrm{~s}$ is:
$d = v \times t$
$d = 4 \times 5 = 20 \mathrm{~m}$

Answer: $20 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A body of mass $m$ moving along the positive x-axis with speed $v$ collides completely inelastically with another identical body of mass $m$ moving along the positive y-axis with the same speed $v$. What is the magnitude of the velocity of the combined mass immediately after the collision?
questions.solution:
The initial momentum of the system is the vector sum of the momenta of the two bodies.

Initial momentum vector, $\vec{p}_i = m v \hat{i} + m v \hat{j}$

The magnitude of the initial momentum is:
$|\vec{p}_i| = \sqrt{(mv)^2 + (mv)^2} = \sqrt{2} m v$

In a completely inelastic collision, the bodies stick together, so the total mass becomes $m + m = 2m$. Let the final velocity be $\vec{v}_f$.

Final momentum vector, $\vec{p}_f = (2m) \vec{v}_f$

By conservation of linear momentum, $\vec{p}_i = \vec{p}_f$. Therefore, their magnitudes must also be equal:
$|\vec{p}_f| = |\vec{p}_i|$

$(2m) |\vec{v}_f| = \sqrt{2} m v$

$|\vec{v}_f| = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} m v}{2m} = \dfrac{v}{\sqrt{2}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{v}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a light body and a heavy body have the same linear momentum, the light body will cover a greater distance in a given time interval.
Reason (R): For a given linear momentum, the velocity of a body is inversely proportional to its mass.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Linear momentum is given by $p = mv$, which implies $v = \dfrac{p}{m}$.

For a constant linear momentum $p$, the velocity $v$ is inversely proportional to the mass $m$ ($v \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$). Therefore, a light body (smaller mass) will have a greater velocity compared to a heavy body. This makes the Reason (R) correct.

The distance covered in a given time interval $t$ is $d = vt$. Since the light body has a greater velocity, it will cover a greater distance in the same time interval. This makes the Assertion (A) correct.

The Reason (R) provides the exact formulaic relationship that explains why the light body has a higher velocity and consequently covers more distance. Thus, (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ moving with velocity $v$ collides completely inelastically with a stationary particle of mass $3m$. The percentage loss in the kinetic energy of the system due to the collision is:
questions.solution:
Using the principle of conservation of linear momentum:

Initial momentum = Final momentum
$m v + (3m)(0) = (m + 3m) v_f$
$m v = 4m v_f$
$v_f = \dfrac{v}{4}$

Initial kinetic energy of the system:
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

Final kinetic energy of the combined system:
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2} (4m) v_f^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} (4m) \left(\dfrac{v}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{K_i}{4}$

Loss in kinetic energy:
$\Delta K = K_i - K_f = K_i - \dfrac{K_i}{4} = \dfrac{3K_i}{4}$

Percentage loss in kinetic energy:
$\dfrac{\Delta K}{K_i} \times 100 = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 100 = 75\%$

Answer: $75\%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Two particles of masses $m$ and $2m$ start moving simultaneously from the same point on a smooth horizontal circular track in opposite directions. Both particles move with the same constant speed $v$. What is the magnitude of the total linear momentum of the two-particle system at the instant when each particle has covered an angular distance of $45^{\circ}$ from the starting point?
questions.solution:
Let the particles start from the point $(R, 0)$ on a circular track of radius $R$ centered at the origin.

The first particle (mass $m$) moves counter-clockwise. When it covers an angular distance of $45^{\circ}$, its position vector makes an angle of $+45^{\circ}$ with the x-axis. Its velocity vector is tangential to the circular path, making an angle of $45^{\circ} + 90^{\circ} = 135^{\circ}$ with the positive x-axis.

The second particle (mass $2m$) moves clockwise. When it covers an angular distance of $45^{\circ}$, its position vector makes an angle of $-45^{\circ}$ with the x-axis. Its velocity vector is tangential, making an angle of $-45^{\circ} - 90^{\circ} = -135^{\circ}$ with the positive x-axis.

The angle between the two velocity vectors is $135^{\circ} - (-135^{\circ}) = 270^{\circ}$, which is geometrically equivalent to $90^{\circ}$. Thus, the velocity vectors are perpendicular to each other.

The magnitude of the linear momentum of the first particle is $p_1 = mv$.

The magnitude of the linear momentum of the second particle is $p_2 = 2mv$.

Since the two momentum vectors are perpendicular, the magnitude of the total linear momentum of the system is the vector sum:
$P = \sqrt{p_1^2 + p_2^2} = \sqrt{(mv)^2 + (2mv)^2} = \sqrt{m^2v^2 + 4m^2v^2} = \sqrt{5}mv$.

Answer: $\sqrt{5}mv$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A ball of mass $0.5 \text{ kg}$, initially at rest on the ground, is hit vertically upwards by a bat. The upward force exerted by the bat on the ball increases linearly from zero to a maximum value of $100 \text{ N}$ in $0.05 \text{ s}$, and then decreases linearly to zero in the next $0.05 \text{ s}$. Assuming the effect of gravity is negligible during the impact, the maximum height reached by the ball is (Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$):
questions.solution:
The impulse imparted to the ball is equal to the area under the Force-Time graph.

Since the force increases and then decreases linearly, the graph forms a triangle with base $\Delta t = 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.1 \text{ s}$ and height $F_{\text{max}} = 100 \text{ N}$.

Impulse, $J = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.1 \times 100 = 5 \text{ N s}$.

According to the impulse-momentum theorem, $J = \Delta p = m v - 0$.

$5 = 0.5 \times v \Rightarrow v = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The maximum height reached by the ball is given by kinematics:
$h = \dfrac{v^2}{2g} = \dfrac{(10)^2}{2 \times 10} = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5 \text{ m}$.

Answer: $5 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
A bomb of mass $4m$ at rest explodes into 3 pieces of masses $m$, $m$, and $2m$. The two pieces of mass $m$ move with speed $v$ perpendicular to each other. Match the quantities in List-I with their corresponding values in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Magnitude of momentum of the heaviest fragment(I) $\dfrac{v}{\sqrt{2}}$
(B) Speed of the heaviest fragment(II) $\sqrt{2} m v$
(C) Kinetic energy of the heaviest fragment(III) $\dfrac{3}{2} m v^2$
(D) Total kinetic energy generated in the explosion(IV) $\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
By the law of conservation of linear momentum, the initial momentum of the bomb is zero. Thus, the vector sum of the momenta of the three fragments must be zero.

Let the two fragments of mass $m$ move along the x and y axes. Their momenta are $\vec{p}_1 = m v \hat{i}$ and $\vec{p}_2 = m v \hat{j}$.

The momentum of the heaviest fragment (mass $2m$) is $\vec{p}_3 = -(\vec{p}_1 + \vec{p}_2) = -m v \hat{i} - m v \hat{j}$.

Magnitude of momentum of the heaviest fragment: $p_3 = \sqrt{(mv)^2 + (mv)^2} = \sqrt{2} m v$. (Matches II)

Speed of the heaviest fragment: $v_3 = \dfrac{p_3}{2m} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} m v}{2m} = \dfrac{v}{\sqrt{2}}$. (Matches I)

Kinetic energy of the heaviest fragment: $K_3 = \dfrac{p_3^2}{2(2m)} = \dfrac{2 m^2 v^2}{4m} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$. (Matches IV)

Total kinetic energy generated: $K_{total} = K_1 + K_2 + K_3 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{3}{2} m v^2$. (Matches III)

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A block of mass $2$ kg moving with a speed of $4$ m s$^{-1}$ on a frictionless horizontal surface collides elastically with an identical block initially at rest. The second block is attached to one end of a relaxed ideal spring of spring constant $32$ N m$^{-1}$, with its other end fixed to a rigid wall. The maximum compression of the spring is:
questions.solution:
Since the collision is perfectly elastic and the blocks have identical masses, they exchange their velocities upon collision.

Velocity of the second block just after the collision, $v = 4$ m s$^{-1}$.

By conservation of mechanical energy for the second block and spring system:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2$

Substituting the given values ($m = 2$ kg, $v = 4$ m s$^{-1}$, $k = 32$ N m$^{-1}$):

$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (4)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 32 \times x^2$

$16 = 16 x^2$

$x^2 = 1 \Rightarrow x = 1$ m.

Answer: $1$ m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ sliding with speed $v$ on a smooth horizontal surface collides head-on and elastically with a stationary block of mass $2m$. Immediately after the collision, the first block enters a rough patch with a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu$. The stopping distance of the first block after it enters the rough patch is (acceleration due to gravity is $g$):
questions.solution:
For a one-dimensional elastic collision, the velocity of the first block after the collision is given by:
$v_1 = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u_1$

Substituting the given values ($m_1 = m$, $m_2 = 2m$, $u_1 = v$):
$v_1 = \dfrac{m - 2m}{m + 2m}v = -\dfrac{v}{3}$

The negative sign indicates that the first block rebounds with a speed of $\dfrac{v}{3}$.

When this block enters the rough patch, the kinetic friction provides a retardation $a = \mu g$.
Using the third equation of motion ($v_f^2 = v_i^2 - 2as$) with final velocity $v_f = 0$:
$0 = \left(\dfrac{v}{3}\right)^2 - 2(\mu g)s$

$s = \dfrac{\dfrac{v^2}{9}}{2\mu g} = \dfrac{v^2}{18\mu g}$

Answer: $\dfrac{v^2}{18\mu g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Two bodies, A and B, are moving with uniform velocities. The ratio of their masses is $1 : 4$ and the ratio of their linear momenta is $2 : 1$. The ratio of the distances covered by them in the same time interval is:
questions.solution:
Let the masses of bodies A and B be $m_{\text{A}}$ and $m_{\text{B}}$, and their linear momenta be $p_{\text{A}}$ and $p_{\text{B}}$.

Given:
$\dfrac{m_{\text{A}}}{m_{\text{B}}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$
$\dfrac{p_{\text{A}}}{p_{\text{B}}} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

The velocity of a body is given by $v = \dfrac{p}{m}$.
The distance covered in time $t$ is $d = v \times t = \dfrac{p}{m} \times t$.

Since the time interval $t$ is the same for both bodies, the ratio of distances covered is:
$\dfrac{d_{\text{A}}}{d_{\text{B}}} = \dfrac{p_{\text{A}} / m_{\text{A}}}{p_{\text{B}} / m_{\text{B}}} = \left( \dfrac{p_{\text{A}}}{p_{\text{B}}} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{m_{\text{B}}}{m_{\text{A}}} \right)$

Substituting the given values:
$\dfrac{d_{\text{A}}}{d_{\text{B}}} = \left( \dfrac{2}{1} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{4}{1} \right) = \dfrac{8}{1}$

Hence, the ratio of the distances covered is $8 : 1$.

Answer: $8 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A projectile of mass $M$ is fired from the ground with an initial speed $u$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. At the highest point of its trajectory, it explodes into two fragments of mass $\dfrac{M}{3}$ and $\dfrac{2M}{3}$. If the lighter fragment comes to rest immediately after the explosion, the extra energy released during the explosion is
questions.solution:
At the highest point of the trajectory, the vertical component of velocity is zero. The horizontal component of velocity is:
$v_x = u \cos 60^{\circ} = \dfrac{u}{2}$

The kinetic energy of the projectile just before the explosion is:
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} M \left(\dfrac{u}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{M u^2}{8}$

The momentum of the projectile just before the explosion is entirely horizontal:
$p_i = M \left(\dfrac{u}{2}\right) = \dfrac{M u}{2}$

Let $v_f$ be the velocity of the heavier fragment (mass $\dfrac{2M}{3}$) after the explosion. Since the lighter fragment (mass $\dfrac{M}{3}$) comes to rest, its momentum is zero.

By conservation of linear momentum along the horizontal direction:
$p_i = p_f$
$\dfrac{M u}{2} = \left(\dfrac{M}{3}\right)(0) + \left(\dfrac{2M}{3}\right) v_f$
$\implies v_f = \dfrac{3 u}{4}$

The kinetic energy of the system just after the explosion is:
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{2M}{3}\right) \left(\dfrac{3 u}{4}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{M}{3}\right) \left(\dfrac{9 u^2}{16}\right) = \dfrac{3 M u^2}{16}$

The extra energy released during the explosion is the increase in kinetic energy:
$\Delta K = K_f - K_i = \dfrac{3 M u^2}{16} - \dfrac{M u^2}{8} = \dfrac{3 M u^2 - 2 M u^2}{16} = \dfrac{M u^2}{16}$

Answer: $\dfrac{M u^2}{16}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A block of mass $m_1$ moving with a velocity $v$ on a smooth horizontal surface collides completely inelastically with another block of mass $m_2$ which is initially at rest. If the combined system moves with a velocity of $\dfrac{v}{5}$ after the collision, what is the ratio of their masses $m_1 : m_2$?
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of linear momentum, the initial momentum of the system is equal to the final momentum.

Initial momentum $= m_1 v + m_2(0) = m_1 v$

Since the collision is completely inelastic, the two blocks stick together and move with a common velocity.

Final momentum $= (m_1 + m_2) \left(\dfrac{v}{5}\right)$

Equating initial and final momentum:
$m_1 v = (m_1 + m_2) \left(\dfrac{v}{5}\right)$

Cancelling $v$ from both sides and cross-multiplying:
$5m_1 = m_1 + m_2$

$4m_1 = m_2$

$\dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Thus, the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ is $1:4$.

Answer: $1:4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A particle of mass $250 \mathrm{~g}$ covers a distance of $120 \mathrm{~m}$ in $4 \mathrm{~s}$ while moving at a constant speed. The linear momentum of the particle is:
questions.solution:
Given,
$m = 250 \mathrm{~g} = 0.25 \mathrm{~kg}$
$d = 120 \mathrm{~m}$
$t = 4 \mathrm{~s}$

The velocity of the particle is:
$v = \dfrac{d}{t} = \dfrac{120}{4} = 30 \mathrm{~m/s}$

The linear momentum $p$ is given by:
$p = m \times v$
$p = 0.25 \times 30 = 7.5 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

Answer: $7.5 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Two particles of equal mass $m$ start moving simultaneously from the same point on a horizontal circular track of radius $R$. They move in opposite directions with the same constant speed $v$. What is the angular distance $\phi$ covered by each particle from the starting point at the instant when the magnitude of the total linear momentum of the two-particle system exactly equals the momentum of a single particle?
questions.solution:
Let the particles start from the position $(0, R)$ on the circular track. At any instant, let each particle have covered an angular distance $\phi$.

The velocity of the first particle (moving clockwise) is $\vec{v}_1 = v\cos\phi \hat{i} - v\sin\phi \hat{j}$.

The velocity of the second particle (moving counter-clockwise) is $\vec{v}_2 = -v\cos\phi \hat{i} - v\sin\phi \hat{j}$.

The total linear momentum of the system is $\vec{P} = m\vec{v}_1 + m\vec{v}_2 = -2mv\sin\phi \hat{j}$.

The magnitude of the total momentum is $P = 2mv\sin\phi$.

We are given that $P$ equals the momentum of a single particle, which is $mv$.

Therefore, $2mv\sin\phi = mv$

$\sin\phi = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

A common mistake is assuming the angle between the velocity vectors is $2\phi$ such that $P = 2mv\cos\phi$, which incorrectly leads to $\phi = \pi/3$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A moving body always rebounds in the opposite direction after a head-on elastic collision with a stationary target of a different mass.
Reason (R): In a one-dimensional elastic collision, a moving body of mass $m$ transfers the exact same fraction of its initial kinetic energy to a stationary target of mass $2m$ as it does to a stationary target of mass $m/2$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Evaluate Assertion (A):
The final velocity of a moving body of mass $m_1$ colliding elastically with a stationary target of mass $m_2$ is $v_1 = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u_1$.
The body only rebounds (i.e., $v_1$ is negative) if $m_1 \lt m_2$. If $m_1 \gt m_2$, it continues moving in the same direction. Therefore, it does not always rebound when the masses are different. Assertion (A) is false.

Evaluate Reason (R):
The fraction of kinetic energy transferred to a stationary target is $f = \dfrac{4m_1 m_2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2}$.
For a target of mass $2m$: $f = \dfrac{4(m)(2m)}{(m + 2m)^2} = \dfrac{8m^2}{9m^2} = \dfrac{8}{9}$.
For a target of mass $m/2$: $f = \dfrac{4(m)(m/2)}{(m + m/2)^2} = \dfrac{2m^2}{(1.5m)^2} = \dfrac{2}{2.25} = \dfrac{8}{9}$.
The fraction transferred is identical in both cases. Reason (R) is true.

Thus, (A) is false but (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Block A of mass $2$ kg moving at $10$ m s$^{-1}$ on a smooth horizontal surface hits Block B of mass $2$ kg initially at rest. The collision is perfectly elastic. Immediately after the collision, Block B enters a rough horizontal surface with a coefficient of kinetic friction $0.5$. Taking $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$, the distance Block B slides before coming to rest is:
questions.solution:
Since the collision is perfectly elastic and the masses of Block A and Block B are equal, they exchange their velocities.

Velocity of Block B just after the collision, $v = 10$ m s$^{-1}$.

As Block B slides on the rough surface, it experiences a retardation $a = \mu g$.

$a = 0.5 \times 10 = 5$ m s$^{-2}$

Using the equation of motion $v_f^2 = v^2 - 2as$ for the stopping distance $s$ (where final velocity $v_f = 0$):

$0 = (10)^2 - 2 \times 5 \times s$

$100 = 10 s$

$s = 10$ m.

Answer: $10$ m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
A moving body of mass $M$ with velocity $v_0 \hat{i}$ explodes into two fragments of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$. Immediately after the explosion, the fragment of mass $m_1$ comes to rest. Match the mass ratios given in List-I with the corresponding final velocity of the second fragment given in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) $1:1$(I) $1.5 v_0 \hat{i}$
(B) $1:2$(II) $2 v_0 \hat{i}$
(C) $2:1$(III) $3 v_0 \hat{i}$
(D) $3:1$(IV) $4 v_0 \hat{i}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of linear momentum, the total initial momentum equals the total final momentum.

$(m_1 + m_2) v_0 \hat{i} = m_1 (0) + m_2 v_2$

$v_2 = \dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{m_2} v_0 \hat{i} = \left(\dfrac{m_1}{m_2} + 1\right) v_0 \hat{i}$

For (A) $m_1:m_2 = 1:1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = 1 \Rightarrow v_2 = (1 + 1) v_0 \hat{i} = 2 v_0 \hat{i}$ (Matches II)

For (B) $m_1:m_2 = 1:2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = 0.5 \Rightarrow v_2 = (0.5 + 1) v_0 \hat{i} = 1.5 v_0 \hat{i}$ (Matches I)

For (C) $m_1:m_2 = 2:1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = 2 \Rightarrow v_2 = (2 + 1) v_0 \hat{i} = 3 v_0 \hat{i}$ (Matches III)

For (D) $m_1:m_2 = 3:1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = 3 \Rightarrow v_2 = (3 + 1) v_0 \hat{i} = 4 v_0 \hat{i}$ (Matches IV)

Therefore, the correct matching is (A) - II, (B) - I, (C) - III, (D) - IV.

Answer: (A) - II, (B) - I, (C) - III, (D) - IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A bomb initially at rest explodes into three pieces. Two pieces, each of mass $m$, fly off at right angles to each other with the same speed $v$. If the total kinetic energy generated in the explosion is $\dfrac{3}{2}mv^2$, what was the total original mass of the bomb?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the third fragment be $m_3$ and its velocity be $\vec{v}_3$.

The first two fragments have mass $m$ and speed $v$, moving at right angles. Their momenta are $m v \hat{i}$ and $m v \hat{j}$.

By conservation of linear momentum:
$\vec{p}_{initial} = \vec{p}_{final}$
$0 = m v \hat{i} + m v \hat{j} + m_3 \vec{v}_3$
$\implies m_3 \vec{v}_3 = -m v \hat{i} - m v \hat{j}$

The magnitude of the momentum of the third fragment is:
$p_3 = \sqrt{(mv)^2 + (mv)^2} = \sqrt{2}mv$

The kinetic energy of the third fragment is:
$K_3 = \dfrac{p_3^2}{2m_3} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{2}mv)^2}{2m_3} = \dfrac{m^2v^2}{m_3}$

The total kinetic energy released is the sum of the kinetic energies of all three fragments:
$K_{total} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + K_3 = mv^2 + \dfrac{m^2v^2}{m_3}$

Given that $K_{total} = \dfrac{3}{2}mv^2$:
$mv^2 + \dfrac{m^2v^2}{m_3} = \dfrac{3}{2}mv^2$
$\implies \dfrac{m^2v^2}{m_3} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$
$\implies m_3 = 2m$

The total original mass of the bomb is $m + m + 2m = 4m$.

Answer: $4m$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A projectile moving with velocity $v$ explodes into two equal fragments. If one fragment is observed to move with velocity $3v$, the other fragment must be moving with velocity $v$.

Reason (R): The velocity of the center of mass of a system remains unchanged during an explosion because the forces of explosion are internal forces.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct
questions.solution:
Evaluate Assertion (A): By conservation of linear momentum, the total initial momentum equals the total final momentum.

Let the total mass of the projectile be $m$.

$m v = \dfrac{m}{2} (3v) + \dfrac{m}{2} v_2$

$v = 1.5v + 0.5 v_2 \Rightarrow -0.5v = 0.5 v_2 \Rightarrow v_2 = -v$

The other fragment must move with velocity $-v$, not $v$. Thus, the Assertion is incorrect.

Evaluate Reason (R): During an explosion, the forces involved are purely internal. Since there is no net external force acting on the system, the acceleration of the center of mass is zero, and its velocity remains unchanged. Thus, the Reason is correct.

Therefore, Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.

Answer: Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Two identical particles start simultaneously from the same point on a smooth horizontal circular track and move in opposite directions with equal constant speeds. The magnitude of the acceleration of their center of mass is maximum at the instant they meet again.
Reason (R): At the instant the particles meet again, the total linear momentum of the two-particle system is zero.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
Let the particles start from $\theta = 0$ and move with angular speed $\omega$ on a track of radius $R$.

The position vectors of the two particles at time $t$ are $\vec{r}_1 = R\cos(\omega t)\hat{i} + R\sin(\omega t)\hat{j}$ and $\vec{r}_2 = R\cos(\omega t)\hat{i} - R\sin(\omega t)\hat{j}$.

The position of the center of mass is $\vec{r}_{cm} = \dfrac{m\vec{r}_1 + m\vec{r}_2}{2m} = R\cos(\omega t)\hat{i}$.

The acceleration of the center of mass is $\vec{a}_{cm} = \dfrac{d^2\vec{r}_{cm}}{dt^2} = -\omega^2 R\cos(\omega t)\hat{i}$.

The particles meet again when they have each covered an angle of $\pi$, i.e., $\omega t = \pi$. At this instant, the magnitude of the acceleration of the center of mass is $|\vec{a}_{cm}| = \omega^2 R |\cos(\pi)| = \omega^2 R$, which is its maximum possible value. Alternatively, the net external force on the system is the vector sum of the centripetal forces provided by the track. When the particles meet, these forces are parallel and add up to a maximum value, leading to maximum acceleration of the center of mass. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

The velocity of the center of mass is $\vec{v}_{cm} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}_{cm}}{dt} = -\omega R\sin(\omega t)\hat{i}$.

At the instant they meet ($\omega t = \pi$), $\vec{v}_{cm} = 0$, so the total linear momentum of the system is zero. Thus, Reason (R) is true.

However, the total linear momentum being zero (a kinematic condition of velocity) is not the cause of the acceleration being maximum. The maximum acceleration is due to the alignment of the external centripetal forces. Therefore, Reason (R) does not correctly explain Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A stationary nucleus of mass number $A$ undergoes alpha decay by emitting an alpha particle of mass $4$. If the total kinetic energy released in the reaction is $Q$, what is the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter nucleus?
questions.solution:
Let the momentum of the emitted alpha particle be $p$. By the law of conservation of linear momentum, the recoiling daughter nucleus must have an equal and opposite momentum of magnitude $p$.

The mass of the alpha particle is $4$ and the mass of the daughter nucleus is $(A-4)$.

The kinetic energy of the alpha particle is $K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{p^2}{2(4)}$ and the kinetic energy of the daughter nucleus is $K_D = \dfrac{p^2}{2(A-4)}$.

The total kinetic energy released is $Q = K_{\alpha} + K_D = \dfrac{p^2}{2(4)} + \dfrac{p^2}{2(A-4)}$.

Simplifying the expression for $Q$:
$Q = \dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{A-4} \right) = \dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{A-4+4}{4(A-4)} \right) = \dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{A}{4(A-4)} \right)$.

We need to find $K_D$ in terms of $Q$. Taking the ratio:
$\dfrac{K_D}{Q} = \dfrac{\dfrac{p^2}{2(A-4)}}{\dfrac{p^2}{2} \left( \dfrac{A}{4(A-4)} \right)} = \dfrac{4}{A}$.

Thus, the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter nucleus is $K_D = \dfrac{4Q}{A}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4Q}{A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A ball of mass $0.2 \text{ kg}$ is dropped from a height of $20 \text{ m}$. Upon striking the ground, the ground imparts an upward impulse of $12 \text{ N s}$ to the ball. The height to which the ball rebounds is $(g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2})$ :
questions.solution:
Velocity of the ball just before striking the ground:
$v_1 = \sqrt{2gh_1} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 20} = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ (downwards)

Taking the upward direction as positive, the initial momentum of the ball is:
$p_i = m(-v_1) = 0.2 \times (-20) = -4 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$

According to the impulse-momentum theorem:
$J = p_f - p_i$
$12 = p_f - (-4)$
$12 = p_f + 4 \Rightarrow p_f = 8 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$

The rebound velocity $v_2$ is:
$v_2 = \dfrac{p_f}{m} = \dfrac{8}{0.2} = 40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ (upwards)

The height to which the ball rebounds is:
$h_2 = \dfrac{v_2^2}{2g} = \dfrac{40^2}{2 \times 10} = \dfrac{1600}{20} = 80 \text{ m}$

Answer: $80 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $L$ has a bob of mass $m$. It is released from rest from a horizontal position. At the lowest point of its swing, the bob makes a head-on elastic collision with a stationary block of mass $3m$ resting on a smooth horizontal surface. The maximum height reached by the pendulum bob as it rebounds after the collision is
questions.solution:
Let the velocity of the pendulum bob just before the collision be $u$. By conservation of mechanical energy, as it falls from a horizontal position (height $L$):
$u = \sqrt{2gL}$

The collision is head-on and elastic. The velocity $v_1$ of the bob of mass $m$ after colliding with a stationary block of mass $3m$ is:
$v_1 = \left( \dfrac{m - 3m}{m + 3m} \right) u$
$v_1 = \left( \dfrac{-2m}{4m} \right) u = -\dfrac{u}{2}$

The negative sign indicates that the bob rebounds. Its speed after the collision is $\dfrac{u}{2}$.

Let the maximum height reached by the bob during its rebound be $h$. Using conservation of mechanical energy again:
$\dfrac{1}{2}m v_1^2 = mgh$

Substituting $v_1 = \dfrac{u}{2}$ and $u^2 = 2gL$:
$\dfrac{1}{2}m \left( \dfrac{u}{2} \right)^2 = mgh$
$\dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{u^2}{4} \right) = gh$
$\dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{2gL}{4} \right) = gh$
$\dfrac{gL}{4} = gh$

$\Rightarrow h = \dfrac{L}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{L}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A very heavy block of mass $M$ moving horizontally with a speed of $2$ ms$^{-1}$ elastically collides with a small pendulum bob of mass $m$ initially at rest, where $M \gg m$. The bob is suspended by a light string. Taking $g = 10$ ms$^{-2}$, the maximum vertical height reached by the pendulum bob after the collision is:
questions.solution:
In a 1D elastic collision where a very heavy object ($M$) collides with a light stationary object ($m$), the light object acquires approximately twice the initial velocity of the heavy object.

$v_{\text{bob}} = 2v = 2 \times 2 = 4$ ms$^{-1}$.

By conservation of mechanical energy for the pendulum swing, the kinetic energy of the bob just after the collision is converted entirely into gravitational potential energy at its maximum height:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v_{\text{bob}}^2 = mgh$

$h = \dfrac{v_{\text{bob}}^2}{2g} = \dfrac{4^2}{2 \times 10} = \dfrac{16}{20} = 0.8$ m.

Answer: $0.8$ m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A ball of mass $0.3 \text{ kg}$ strikes a rigid vertical wall with a speed of $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ with the surface of the wall. It rebounds with the same speed and at the same angle. The magnitude of the impulse imparted to the ball by the wall is:
questions.solution:
Let the wall be along the y-axis and the normal to the wall be along the x-axis.

The angle made by the velocity vector with the surface of the wall is $\theta = 30^\circ$.

The component of velocity perpendicular to the wall is $v_{\perp} = v \sin 30^\circ$.
The component of velocity parallel to the wall is $v_{\parallel} = v \cos 30^\circ$.

During the collision, the parallel component remains unchanged, while the perpendicular component reverses its direction.

Initial momentum perpendicular to the wall, $p_{i} = m v \sin 30^\circ$
Final momentum perpendicular to the wall, $p_{f} = -m v \sin 30^\circ$

Magnitude of impulse = Change in momentum = $|p_{f} - p_{i}| = 2 m v \sin 30^\circ$

Impulse $= 2 \times 0.3 \times 10 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 3 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $3 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A gun applies a force $F$ on a bullet which is given by $F=\left(100-0.5 \times 10^5 t\right) \mathrm{N}$. The bullet emerges out with speed $400 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Then find out the impulse exerted till force on bullet becomes zero
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text { (c) : Given, force } F=\left(100-0.5 \times 10^5 t\right) \mathrm{N} \\ & 100-0.5 \times 10^5 t=0,100=0.5 \times 10^5 t(\because F=0) \\ & t=2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{sec} \\ & \text { Impulse, } I=\int F d t=\int_0^{2 \times 10^{-3}}\left(100-0.5 \times 10^5 t\right) d t \\ & I=\left[100 t-\frac{10^5}{2} \frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^{2 \times 10^{-3}} \\ & I=\left[100 \times 2 \times 10^{-3}-\frac{10^5}{4} \times 4 \times 10^{-6}\right] \\ & I=10^{-1}=0.1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~s}\end{aligned}$

questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Body $A$ of mass $4 m$ moving with speed $u$ collides with another body $B$ of mass $2 m$ at rest. The collision is head on and elastic in nature. After the collision the fraction of energy lost by colliding body $A$ is
questions.solution:
Energy transferred to $B$.
Initial energy of $B=$ zero
Final velocity of
$\begin{aligned} & v_B=\left(\frac{m_2-m_1}{m_1+m_2}\right) u_2+\frac{2 m_1 u_1}{m_1+m_2} \\ & m_1=4 m, u_1=u \\ & m_2=2 m, u_2=0 \\ & v_B=\frac{2(4 m) u}{6 m}=\frac{4}{3} u \\ & \frac{\frac{1}{2} m_2 v_B^2}{\frac{1}{2} m_1 u_1^2}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} 2 m\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2 u^2}{\frac{1}{2} 4 m u^2} \\ & \end{aligned}$
Fraction of energy lost $=8 / 9$

questions.q: A spacecraft of mass $100 \mathrm{~kg}$ breaks into two when its velocity is $10^4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. After the break, a mass of $10 \mathrm{~kg}$ of the spacecraft is left stationary. The velocity of the remaining part is

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A body of mass $m_1$ collides elastically with another body of mass $m_2$ at rest. If the velocity of $m_1$ after collision becomes $2 / 3$ times its initial velocity, the ratio of their masses is
questions.solution:
Let $v$ be the initial velocity of body of mass $m_1$ before collision. Since collision is elastic both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. $\therefore m_1 v=m_1 \frac{2}{3} v+m_2 v_2$ or $m_1\left(v-\frac{2}{3} v\right)=m_2 v_2$
Also, $\frac{1}{2} m_1 v^2=\frac{1}{2} m_1\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 v^2+\frac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2$ or $m_1\left(v^2-\frac{4}{9} v^2\right)=m_2 v_2^2$ or $\frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{9 v_2^2}{5 v^2}$ Equating (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} & \frac{9 v_2^2}{5 v^2}=\frac{3 v_2}{v} \text { or } \frac{v_2}{v}=\frac{5}{3} \\ & \therefore \frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{3 \times 5}{3}=\frac{5}{1}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Height covered in $1 \mathrm{~min}$,
$s_1=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2=0+\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times(60)^2=18000 \mathrm{~m}$
Velocity attained after $1 \mathrm{~min}$,
$v=u+a t=0+10 \times 60=600 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
After the fuel is finished, $u=600 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}, v=0\begin{aligned} & v^2-u^2=2 g s_2 \\ & \text { or } \quad 0-(600)^2=2 \times(-9.8) \times s_2 \\ & \text { or } \quad s_2=\frac{(600)^2}{2 \times 9.8}=18367.3 \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$
Maximum height reached $=s_1+s_2=36367.3 \mathrm{~m}=36.4 \mathrm{~km}$

questions.q: A bomb moving with velocity $(40 \hat{i}+50 \hat{j}-25 \hat{k}) \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ explodes into two pieces of mass ratio $1: 4$. After explosion the smaller piece moves away with velocity $(200 \hat{i}+70 \hat{j}+15 \hat{k}) \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The velocity of larger piece after explosion is
questions.solution:
( Let the mass of the unexploded bomb be $5 \mathrm{~m}$. It explodes into the two pieces of masses $m$ and $4 m$ respectively.
Initial momentum of the unexploded bomb
$=5 m(40 \hat{i}+50 \hat{j}-25 \hat{k})$
After explosion, momentum of the smaller piece $=m \vec{v}_1=m(200 \hat{i}+70 \hat{j}+15 \hat{k})$ and momentum of the larger piece $=4 m \vec{v}_2$ where $\vec{v}_1$ and $\vec{v}_2$ are the velocities of the two pieces respectively.
According to the law of conservation of momentum, we get
$\begin{aligned} & 5 m(40 \hat{i}+50 \hat{j}-25 \hat{k})=m(200 \hat{i}+70 \hat{j}+15 \hat{k})+4 m \vec{v}_2 \\ & 4 m \vec{v}_2=5 m(40 \hat{i}+50 \hat{j}-25 \hat{k})-m(200 \hat{i}+70 \hat{j}+15 \hat{k}) \\ & \quad \vec{v}_2=\frac{1}{4}(180 \hat{j}-140 \hat{k})=45 \hat{j}-35 \hat{k}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A ball impinges directly on a similar ball at rest. The first ball is brought to rest by the impact. If half of the kinetic energy is lost by impact, the value of coefficient of restitution is
questions.solution:
Let $u_1$ and $v_1$ be the initial and final velocities of ball 1 and $u_2$ and $v_2$ be the similar quantities for ball 2. Here, $u_2=0$ and $v_1=0$.
$\therefore \quad$ initial KE, $K_i=\frac{1}{2} m u_1^2+\frac{1}{2} m u_2^2=\frac{1}{2} m u_1^2$
and final KE, $K_f=\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2+\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2=\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2$
Loss of $\mathrm{KE}, \Delta K=K_i-K_f=\frac{1}{2} m u_1^2-\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2$
According to question,
$\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} m u_1^2\right)=\frac{1}{2} m u_1^2-\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2$
( $\because$ half of its $\mathrm{KE}$ is lost by impact) or $u_1^2=2 v_2^2$ or $v_2=\frac{u_1}{\sqrt{2}}\therefore \quad$ Coefficient of restitution,
$e=\left|\frac{v_2-v_1}{u_1-u_2}\right|=\frac{v_2}{u_1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.q: A neutron makes a head-on elastic collision with a stationary deuteron. The fractional energy loss of the neutron in the collision is
questions.solution: One deuteron consists of one proton and one neutron. As the mass of a proton and a neutron is approximately same $\left(\approx 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}\right)$, we assume that the mass of the neutron be $m$ and the mass of the deuteron be $2 m$ as the electron mass is negligibly small compared to that of proton and neutron. Let the initial velocity of the neutron be $u$. As the deuteron is initially at rest, the final velocity of the neutron is v_1=\left(\frac{m-2 m}{m+2 m}\right) u=-\frac{m u}{3 m}=-\frac{u}{3} . and the velocity of the deuteron is v_2=\frac{2 m}{m+2 m} u=\frac{2}{3} u \text {. } Total energy before collision is $E_1=\frac{1}{2} m u^2$ After collision, the energy gained by the deuteron is E_d=\frac{1}{2} \times(2 m) v_2^2=m \times\left(\frac{2}{3} u\right)^2=\frac{4}{9} m u^2 . $E_d$ is the amount of energy lost by the neutron. Therefore the fractional loss of energy of the neutron is \frac{E_d}{E_1}=\frac{(4 / 9) m u^2}{(1 / 2) m u^2}=\frac{8}{9}

options: four times of the initial value
eight times of the initial value.
questions.solution:
Initial kinetic energy $\left(E_1\right)=E$ and final kinetic energy $\left(E_2\right)=4 E$.
Kinetic energy of a body is $\frac{1}{2} m v^2$
Since the value of $m$ remains constant, therefore for the kinetic energy to be 4 times, the new value of velocity (v) should be 2 times the initial value. Initial linear momentum $\left(p_1\right)=m v$.
Therefore new linear momentum $\left(p_2\right)=m \times 2 v=2 m v=2 p_1$

$\begin{aligned} v^{\prime} & =v \sqrt{\sin ^2 \theta+e^2 \cos ^2 \theta} \\ \text { and } \quad \tan \theta^{\prime} & =\frac{\tan \theta}{e}\end{aligned}$
For elastic collision, $e=1$, so that $\theta^{\prime}=\theta$ and $v^{\prime}=v$

Kinetic energy $=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times(4)^2=96 \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: For inelastic collision between two spherical rigid bodies
options: the total kinetic energy is conserved
the total mechanical energy is not conserved
the linear momentum is not conserved
questions.solution: In an inelastic collision, the particles do not regain their shape and size completely after collision. Some fraction of mechanical energy is retained by the colliding particles in the form of deformation potential energy. Thus, the kinetic energy of particles no longer remains conserved. However in the absence of external forces, law of conservation of linear momentum still holds good.

questions.q: A small disc of radius 2 cm is cut from a disc of radius 6 cm . If the distance between their centres is 3.2 cm , what is the shift in the centre of mass of the disc?
questions.solution: The situation can be shown as : Let radius of complete disc is $a$ and that of small disc is $b$. Also let centre of mass now shifts to $\mathrm{O}_2$ at a distance $x_2$ from original centre. The position of new centre of mass is given by $X_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{-\sigma \cdot \pi b^2 \cdot x_1}{\sigma \cdot \pi a^2-\sigma \cdot \pi b^2}$ Here, $a=6 \mathrm{~cm}, b=2 \mathrm{~cm}, x_1=3.2 \mathrm{~cm}$ Hence, $\quad X_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{-\sigma \times \pi(2)^2 \times 3.2}{\sigma \times \pi \times(6)^2-\sigma \times \pi \times(2)^2}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{12.8 \pi}{32 \pi} \\ & =-0.4 \mathrm{~cm}\end{aligned}$
